nodes.name: Tree ferns
nodes.desc: Tall tree ferns are a hallmark of the wet, misty mountain forest, and many other ferns and epiphytes grow in the same cloud-soaked habitat.

nodes.name: Blue Mountain yacca
nodes.desc: A native conifer of the high Blue Mountain forest, one of the plant species recorded most often in the park area.

nodes.name: Ocotea trees
nodes.desc: Laurel-family forest trees. Female giant swallowtails have been seen laying eggs on Ocotea, and the trees bear fruit that forest animals eat.

nodes.name: Lantana
nodes.desc: A flowering shrub whose nectar is used by the Homerus swallowtail. Hummingbirds and other nectar feeders also visit it.

nodes.name: Homerus swallowtail
nodes.desc: The largest butterfly in the Western Hemisphere. Adults sip nectar and females lay eggs on Ocotea. Blue and John Crow Mountains hold one of its two last populations.

nodes.name: Jamaican hutia
nodes.desc: A night-foraging rodent found only in Jamaica. It eats fruit, roots, bark and leaves from many plants.

nodes.name: Jamaican fruit bat
nodes.desc: Eats mainly fruit, especially figs, and carries it away to eat, which spreads seeds through the forest.

nodes.name: Ring-tailed pigeon
nodes.desc: An endemic forest pigeon of Jamaica that feeds mostly on fruit and was among the most recorded birds near the park.

nodes.name: Red-billed streamertail
nodes.desc: Jamaica's national bird, the most recorded species here. It feeds mainly on nectar and also catches small insects.

nodes.name: Bananaquit
nodes.desc: A small nectar and fruit eater. It pierces flower bases to reach nectar, which other nectar feeders then use.

nodes.name: Forest ants
nodes.desc: Ants are abundant in the leaf litter and on plants. They take nectar and sugary foods and are a main prey for small lizards, frogs and birds.

nodes.name: Stripefoot anole
nodes.desc: A common Jamaican lizard that hunts insects, including ants, and is itself eaten by snakes and mongooses.

nodes.name: Jamaican tody
nodes.desc: A tiny endemic bird that catches insects and other small invertebrates in the forest understory.

nodes.name: Jamaican forest frogs
nodes.desc: Several small frog species recorded in the park that develop without a tadpole stage. They hunt small invertebrates on the forest floor.

nodes.name: Sad flycatcher
nodes.desc: A Jamaican flycatcher that hunts insects. The Jamaican boa is known to eat flycatcher nests.

nodes.name: Small Indian mongoose
nodes.desc: An introduced predator on Jamaica that eats small lizards, frogs and ground-nesting birds, and so competes with native predators.

nodes.name: Turkey vulture
nodes.desc: Called the John crow in Jamaica, which gave the mountains half of their name. It scavenges carrion.

nodes.name: Jamaican boa
nodes.desc: Jamaica's top native predator. It kills by constriction and eats birds, bats and lizards, and hunts from ambush in vines and bromeliads.

nodes.name: Rain and cloud mist
nodes.desc: Heavy rain and constant mist keep humidity high. This is the main driver of the mountain's lush forest.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Light reaching the forest canopy and clearings drives growth of trees, ferns and flowering shrubs.

nodes.name: Mountain soil
nodes.desc: Nutrient-rich soil and leaf litter feed the forest plants, topped up by decomposers.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi, bacteria and litter invertebrates break down dead leaves, wood and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.
